title: Jeremiah 50:1–20
context: Chapters 50–51 form one collection of oracles against Babylon, introduced as the word the LORD spoke “by Jeremiah the prophet” (50:1). The LORD announces that Babylon is taken and its gods shamed by a nation from the north (50:2–3), while Israel and Judah return weeping to seek him in an everlasting covenant (50:4–5). The scattered flock is called to flee Babylon (50:8), and the LORD promises to punish Babylon as he punished Assyria, restore Israel to its pasture, and pardon the remnant (50:17–20). On Babylon as the LORD’s agent who is then judged, see the existing Judges 9:23 box.

verses.text: The word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by Jeremiah the prophet.
verses.arminianNotes: The heading introduces “The word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon … by Jeremiah the prophet.” Arminian readers see the empire that conquered Judah now placed under the same divine judgment it carried out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD as sovereign over the nation he used against Judah. Readers in this tradition note that the oracle is attributed to the LORD and delivered through his prophet, so its announcements rest on his word.

verses.text: “Declare among the nations and publish, and set up a standard; publish, and don’t conceal; say, ‘Babylon has been taken, Bel is disappointed, Merodach is dismayed! Her images are disappointed. Her idols are dismayed.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Babylon has been taken, Bel is disappointed, Merodach is dismayed!” Arminian readers see the fall of the city as the shame of its gods, exposed as unable to save those who trusted them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s triumph over Babylon’s idols. Bel and Merodach are commonly taken as titles of Babylon’s chief god, and readers in this tradition see the oracle as a contest between the living God and false gods.

verses.text: For a nation comes up out of the north against her, which will make her land desolate, and no one will dwell in it. They have fled. They are gone, both man and animal.
verses.arminianNotes: “For a nation comes up out of the north against her.” Arminian readers note the reversal: Judah’s invader from the north now faces an invader from the north, which shows God’s justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reversal of earlier oracles against Judah. The nation is not named here, though later lines mention the Medes (51:11, 28), and readers in this tradition hold detailed identifications with care.

verses.text: “In those days, and in that time,” says the LORD, “the children of Israel will come, they and the children of Judah together; they will go on their way weeping, and will seek the LORD their God.
verses.arminianNotes: “… they will go on their way weeping, and will seek the LORD their God.” Arminian readers see repentance and return joined: Israel and Judah together seek the LORD as Babylon falls.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a return marked by humble seeking. Readers in this tradition note that the reunion of Israel and Judah echoes hopes found elsewhere in Jeremiah, such as 3:18, cited by reference.

verses.text: They will inquire concerning Zion with their faces turned toward it, saying, ‘Come, and join yourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will not be forgotten.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Come, and join yourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will not be forgotten.” Arminian readers hear a call to renewed commitment, freely embraced by a people turning back to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a covenant that will endure, which many in this tradition connect with the new covenant promise of 31:31–34. Readers in both traditions commonly see shared ground here on God’s covenant faithfulness.

verses.text: My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have caused them to go astray. They have turned them away on the mountains. They have gone from mountain to hill. They have forgotten their resting place.
verses.arminianNotes: “My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have caused them to go astray.” Arminian readers see leaders held responsible for misleading the people, as in 23:1–2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the failure of Judah’s rulers and teachers, especially its kings, behind the people’s wandering. The image of a forgotten resting place shows how far they strayed from the LORD.

verses.text: All who found them have devoured them. Their adversaries said, ‘We are not guilty, because they have sinned against the LORD, the habitation of righteousness, even the LORD, the hope of their fathers.’
verses.arminianNotes: The adversaries said, “We are not guilty, because they have sinned against the LORD.” Arminian readers see Israel’s enemies excusing their cruelty by pointing to Israel’s sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the nations’ self-justification. The verse admits Israel’s sin while refusing to let the oppressors off, and readers in this tradition note that God judges both his people and those who abuse them.

verses.text: “Flee out of the middle of Babylon! Go out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be as the male goats before the flocks.
verses.arminianNotes: “Flee out of the middle of Babylon!” Arminian readers see a call to leave the doomed city, like male goats leading the flock, which many apply to separation from evil.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the summons to depart before judgment. Some readers note that Revelation 18:4 takes up a similar call, cited here by reference; readers in this tradition hold that connection as a later reuse.

verses.text: For, behold, I will stir up and cause to come up against Babylon a company of great nations from the north country; and they will set themselves in array against her. She will be taken from there. Their arrows will be as of an expert mighty man. None of them will return in vain.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will stir up and cause to come up against Babylon a company of great nations from the north country.” Arminian readers see God directing nations to judge Babylon while they act by their own aims.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s sovereign direction of history. Readers in this tradition note that the arrows of the invaders “will be as of an expert mighty man,” stressing the certainty of the outcome.

verses.text: Chaldea will be a prey. All who prey on her will be satisfied,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Chaldea will be a prey. All who prey on her will be satisfied,” says the LORD. Arminian readers see the plunderer of nations becoming plunder, a fitting reversal of Babylon’s conduct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Babylon reaping what it sowed. Readers in this tradition stress that the LORD announces the outcome, framing the coming plunder as his judgment.

verses.text: “Because you are glad, because you rejoice, O you who plunder my heritage, because you are wanton as a heifer that treads out the grain, and neigh as strong horses,
verses.arminianNotes: “Because you are glad, because you rejoice, O you who plunder my heritage.” Arminian readers see Babylon judged for its gloating over Judah, not merely for being an instrument.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Babylon’s arrogance and delight in plunder as culpable. Readers in this tradition note that the LORD calls Judah “my heritage,” claiming his people even in their judgment.

verses.text: your mother will be utterly disappointed. She who bore you will be confounded. Behold, she will be the least of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.
verses.arminianNotes: “… your mother will be utterly disappointed. She who bore you will be confounded.” Arminian readers see the shame of the land and nation that produced Babylon’s power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Babylon’s mother land brought low. Readers in this tradition note the reversal of status: the greatest of nations becomes “the least of the nations.”

verses.text: Because of the LORD’s wrath she won’t be inhabited, but she will be wholly desolate. Everyone who goes by Babylon will be astonished, and hiss at all her plagues.
verses.arminianNotes: “Because of the LORD’s wrath she won’t be inhabited, but she will be wholly desolate.” Arminian readers see the poem using the language of total desolation to express the certainty of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a picture of complete ruin. The poem’s imagery is stark, and readers in this tradition read it as prophetic language of judgment rather than as a detailed forecast of every event.

verses.text: Set yourselves in array against Babylon all around, all you who bend the bow; shoot at her. Spare no arrows, for she has sinned against the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “… shoot at her. Spare no arrows, for she has sinned against the LORD.” Arminian readers see the ground of judgment stated plainly: Babylon’s sin against the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment grounded in Babylon’s guilt. Readers in this tradition note that the attackers are summoned by the LORD’s word, though the text holds Babylon responsible for its own sin.

verses.text: Shout against her all around. She has submitted herself. Her bulwarks have fallen. Her walls have been thrown down, for it is the vengeance of the LORD. Take vengeance on her. As she has done, do to her.
verses.arminianNotes: “… it is the vengeance of the LORD. Take vengeance on her. As she has done, do to her.” Arminian readers see divine justice repaying Babylon in proportion to its deeds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the principle of just recompense. Readers in both traditions commonly distinguish the LORD’s vengeance, which is righteous judgment, from personal revenge, which Scripture forbids.

verses.text: Cut off the sower from Babylon, and him who handles the sickle in the time of harvest. For fear of the oppressing sword, they will each return to their own people, and they will each flee to their own land.
verses.arminianNotes: “Cut off the sower from Babylon, and him who handles the sickle in the time of harvest.” Arminian readers see the disruption of ordinary life as part of the city’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the loss of harvest and the flight of foreigners. Readers in this tradition note that those from other lands “will each flee to their own land,” as the empire’s hold on peoples breaks.

verses.text: “Israel is a hunted sheep. The lions have driven him away. First, the king of Assyria devoured him, and now at last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has broken his bones.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Israel is a hunted sheep. The lions have driven him away.” Arminian readers see Israel’s history of suffering under Assyria and then Babylon summarized in the image of a hunted sheep.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see two empires pictured as lions. Readers in this tradition note that the verse names both the king of Assyria and Nebuchadnezzar, placing Babylon in a pattern of judged oppressors.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: “Behold, I will punish the king of Babylon and his land, as I have punished the king of Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I will punish the king of Babylon and his land, as I have punished the king of Assyria.” Arminian readers see God’s consistent justice toward empires that oppress his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fall of Assyria as precedent for Babylon’s fall. Readers in this tradition see God’s rule over the rise and fall of nations, consistent with prophecies such as Isaiah 10:12, cited by reference.

verses.text: I will bring Israel again to his pasture, and he will feed on Carmel and Bashan. His soul will be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will bring Israel again to his pasture, and he will feed on Carmel and Bashan.” Arminian readers see restoration pictured in the fertile regions of the land, a renewed life after exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covenant blessing in the return to rich pasture. Readers in this tradition note the inclusion of northern regions such as Ephraim and Gilead, signaling the restoration of all Israel.

verses.text: In those days, and in that time,” says the LORD, “the iniquity of Israel will be sought for, and there will be none, also the sins of Judah, and they won’t be found; for I will pardon them whom I leave as a remnant.
verses.arminianNotes: “… the iniquity of Israel will be sought for, and there will be none … for I will pardon them whom I leave as a remnant.” Arminian readers see forgiveness so complete that sin cannot be found.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise rejoice in pardon that removes sin entirely. Readers in this tradition connect the promise with the forgiveness of the new covenant in 31:34, cited by reference, and see grace at the heart of restoration.
